selected.name: Boundary and Failure Characterization
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract distinguishes regimes where the method helps, does not help, or changes behavior, with explicit assumptions; score 0 when it presents only universal-sounding success claims.
selected.rationale: R12 characterizes when random permutations are or are not optimal, and R46 analyzes how finite width and loss choice affect double descent.

selected.name: Theory-to-Algorithm Closure
selected.instruction: Give 10 when theoretical analysis directly determines an implementable construction, estimator, or guarantee; give 0 when theory is disconnected from the proposed procedure.
selected.rationale: R15, R30, and R50 each turn technical analysis into a concrete algorithmic design, a connection often under-credited by fixed criteria.

selected.name: Challenges a widely-held assumption or standard practice
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly overturns or complicates a piece of received wisdom or standard practice in the field, versus simply extending or applying accepted practice without challenging any assumption. A 10 states a finding that directly contradicts what practitioners would expect (e.g., a standard component turns out to be unnecessary, or a technique backfires). A 0 straightforwardly builds on accepted assumptions without surprising anyone.
selected.rationale: R51 shows the standard practice of training the final classifier layer is largely unnecessary, and R36 shows GNN structure-aware perturbations can make a model perform worse than an ignorant baseline -- both are dense_high_card_low and both directly upend a standard expectation.
member_names: Challenges a widely-held assumption or standard practice
Removes or inverts a standard default rather than adding to it

selected.name: Resource Accounting
selected.instruction: Give 10 when computational, memory, latency, or deployment constraints are quantified and handled by the core design; give 0 when efficiency is asserted only in general terms.
selected.rationale: R11, R25, and R40 integrate parallelism, latency, and complexity reductions into their technical contributions rather than treating efficiency as an afterthought.

selected.name: Positions against a named strongest prior with a stated inability
selected.instruction: Score the specificity of the comparison target. 10 = the abstract names the actual leading prior method and states precisely what it cannot do or where it fails, in terms concrete enough that the failure could be checked. 5 = a named family of approaches with a general limitation. 0 = the prior work is referred to only as existing approaches, previous methods, or current techniques, and the limitation is that the paper's own idea has not been tried. Number of baselines counted in the evaluation does not count here; only the named target of the argument does.
selected.rationale: R47 names the specific layerwise adaptive scheme and states that it performs poorly for attention models; R06 names the originating graph convolution work and gives two concrete structural limits. Both dense_high_card_low. R26 says existing approaches completely ignore solution multiplicity and R08 compares to previous methods that search for successful trajectories; both are dense_low_card_high, and both would pass a related-work-engagement check on the presence of a contrast rather than on its sharpness.
member_names: Named, precise comparison to specific prior methods
Positions against a named strongest prior with a stated inability

selected.name: Economy of exposition (information per sentence)
selected.instruction: Score how much distinct information each sentence of the abstract carries, independent of topic. A 10 is a short, tight abstract where every sentence adds new, non-redundant content. A 0 is a long abstract that restates the same point multiple ways or pads with generic filler sentences.
selected.rationale: R50 (3 short sentences) and R25 (compact, direct) are the two highest dense_pct rows in the entire 60-item slice, both dense_high_card_low, while longer, more diffusely structured abstracts such as R39 sit dense_low_card_high -- suggesting the dense model rewards terse density that a scorecard, reading criterion by criterion, may not specifically credit.
member_names: Informative density under brevity, no field-importance preamble

selected.name: Headline claim survives the abstract's own qualifiers
selected.instruction: Read the strongest sentence of the abstract, then read the reported details, and score whether the strong sentence still stands. 10 = the lead claim is exactly what the detailed results show; no later sentence narrows it. 5 = the lead claim is broad but the narrowing is stated up front. 0 = a broad superiority claim is made first and later details reduce it to a subset (one dataset out of several, some tasks, comparable or better). Score consistency between claim and detail, not the level of performance.
selected.rationale: R39 leads on outperforming the state of the art and then reveals it holds on one dataset and two of three downstream tasks; R25 claims superior performance and then settles for comparable or higher sample efficiency; R03 asserts new state of the art after listing benchmark counts. All three are dense_low_card_high: itemised criteria for evaluation breadth and for reporting results credit the counts and the disclosures separately, and never compare the headline against the fine print.
member_names: Claim scope matched to evidence scope
Headline claim survives the abstract's own qualifiers

selected.name: Explanatory Insight Beyond Performance
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the work yields a transferable conceptual explanation, diagnostic, or unifying interpretation in addition to a method and measurements; score 0 when it reports improvements without illuminating why they occur.
selected.rationale: R06 reframes representation evaluation through MDL and reveals data-efficiency properties, while R39 unifies several Lipschitz constructions through a common algebraic condition.

selected.name: Multiplicity Modeling
selected.instruction: Give 10 when the method represents multiple valid solutions, futures, or explanations without collapsing them into one target; give 0 when an inherently ambiguous problem is forced into a single answer.
selected.rationale: R22 and R35 directly address stochastic futures and one-of-many solutions, dimensions that standard criteria can over-credit without examining modeling adequacy.

selected.name: Explicit code/artifact release mention
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly states that code, models, or data will be or are publicly released. A 10 states a concrete release (e.g., a GitHub link or explicit 'code is available'). A 0 makes no mention of release or reproducibility artifacts.
selected.rationale: R23 ('Open code for reproducing and extending our results is provided') and R60 ('Code is available at https://github.com/...') both make explicit release statements and both are dense_low_card_high, with R60 among the largest dense/scorecard gaps in the whole slice -- suggesting the scorecard treats a release statement as a quality proxy that dense does not reward.

selected.name: Rhetorical framing as adjudicating a field debate
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract explicitly frames itself as resolving an open question or tension in prior literature, using a direct question or an explicit 'prior work suggests X, but...' setup, versus simply stating 'we propose method M for task T' without any such framing device. A 10 opens with an explicit posed question or named tension the paper will resolve. A 0 states its contribution directly with no debate-framing device.
selected.rationale: R07 opens with 'a recent line of...results has corroborated a widely observed phenomenon...however, is random optimal?' and R54 frames itself as identifying 'potential hazards' in a standard approach -- both dense_low_card_high, suggesting this structural rhetorical device is something a criterion-based scorecard rewards more than the dense reader.
member_names: Rhetorical framing as adjudicating a field debate

selected.name: Structure-Aligned Inductive Bias
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the method encodes a domain structure or invariance that is explicitly connected to the task and empirically examined; score 0 when architectural structure is arbitrary or purely cosmetic.
selected.rationale: R13 connects spectral filters to local and global graph context, and R60 derives graph augmentation from spectral structure rather than uniform random perturbations.

selected.name: Theory is load-bearing: the derivation licenses the method
selected.instruction: Score how tightly the stated theory determines the proposed procedure. 10 = a specific proved statement is what makes the algorithm possible or correct, and the abstract shows the path from the statement to the procedure (an identity that yields a tractable objective, a duality that makes a gradient computable, a proof that one objective equals another). 5 = theory that bounds or justifies a method chosen on other grounds. 0 = formal apparatus, background exposition, or a proof of a property nobody doubted, with the method unchanged if the theory were deleted.
selected.rationale: R58 proves that the divergence between stochastic processes equals a supremum of finite-marginal divergences and then builds the training objective on exactly that; R42 derives the dual form and shows the gradient is explicitly computable; R34 proves the new search gradient optimises the same objective as the reinforcement-learning formulation. All are dense_high_card_low. R23 (dense_low_card_high) advertises a self-contained overview of algebraic topology and design guidance, which reads as strong theoretical content to a checklist but does not force the method.
member_names: Theory is load-bearing: the derivation licenses the method

selected.name: Single-idea compressibility (elegance)
selected.instruction: Score whether the paper's core contribution can be stated as one simple, memorable idea versus a bundle of several loosely-related components. A 10 is a paper whose whole contribution reduces to one clean sentence. A 0 requires listing several separate components/mechanisms (i, ii, iii) to describe what was actually done.
selected.rationale: R51 ('fix the last classifier layer instead of training it') is a single elegant idea and is dense_high_card_low; R39 (PAPO) requires three named components -- encoding, hypernetwork, and size-as-input -- to describe, and is dense_low_card_high.

selected.name: Concrete numeric result density
selected.instruction: Score how many specific, checkable numeric results (percentages, deltas, counts, timings) the abstract reports, independent of how positive or well-supported they are. A 10 packs multiple precise figures (e.g., '10.9% improvement', '5-fold reduction', '76 minutes'). A 0 reports only qualitative adjectives ('significant', 'considerable', 'remarkable') with no numbers at all.
selected.rationale: Rows like R60 (10.9%/12.4% MAE improvement) and R41 (5-fold/2-fold/4x speedups) sit in the dense_low_card_high half despite the underlying contribution being narrow engineering work, suggesting the scorecard is drawn to numeric specificity as a rigor proxy even when dense judges the overall contribution as modest.

selected.name: Artifact-release signaling
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit language promising or linking code, models, datasets, configurations, or other research artifacts; judge only the presence of release signaling, not whether the artifacts are useful or real.
selected.rationale: R06, R10, R21, and R37 explicitly mention released code, models, configurations, or pretrained weights. Access to infrastructure and release practices may influence both textual reception and genuine research execution, so this is a mixed nuisance.
member_names: Advertised code, model and dataset release
Explicit code or artifact release statement
upstream_parent_all_members: engineering support and institutional infrastructure available to the producing group

selected.name: Density of formal mathematical/symbolic notation
selected.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much specialized mathematical/symbolic notation appears (inline formulas, Greek letters, subscripts/superscripts, big-O/tilde-O expressions, set/space notation like R^d). Score 0 if the text is plain prose with no symbolic notation, and 10 if the text is dense with symbolic expressions throughout. Do NOT judge whether the mathematics is correct, rigorous, or important -- score only how much symbolic notation is visibly present in the text.
selected.rationale: R48 is thick with expressions like 'epsilon-coreset of size O(m + poly(k eps^{-1}))' (dense_pct=.474, card_pct=.030) and R54 reports a bound 'O~(d^2 H^5 / eps^2)' (dense_pct=.278, card_pct=.004) -- both dense_high_card_low with near-floor card percentiles -- whereas prose-only, notation-free abstracts like R05 and R25 (both dense_low_card_high) contain no inline formulas at all.

selected.name: Density of specific quantified result figures
selected.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of explicitly quantified outcome figures in the text. Count numerals attached to results: percentages, absolute metric values (accuracy, AP, mIoU, FID, MAE), speedup or reduction factors (for example five-fold, two to three orders of magnitude), parameter, FLOP or batch-size counts, wall-clock times, and dataset sizes. Anchors: 0 = no such numerals anywhere; 3 = one figure; 5 = two or three; 8 = four or five; 10 = six or more distinct quantified figures, several carried to one or two decimal places. Score PRESENCE AND DENSITY of numbers only. Do not assess whether the numbers are large, impressive, fairly compared, correctly computed, or whether the gains would matter to anyone.
selected.rationale: A criterion bank almost always contains items that ask whether results are concrete and quantified, so numeral density converts directly into card score independent of what the numerals mean. R14 carries six percentage figures (40 percent, 0.5 percent, 2.8 percent, 43 percent, 0.8 percent, 3 percent) at card 0.923 versus dense 0.372; R21 reports 10.9 percent and 12.4 percent MAE improvements at card 0.974 versus dense 0.094; R36 stacks 1.6 percent Top-1, 0.16M parameters, 0.07B FLOPs and 3-4 percent AP at card 0.868 versus dense 0.415; R26 quotes 6.12 percent and 96.32 percent at card 0.564 versus dense 0.158. The dense model prices all four far lower. Tagged mixed because genuinely strong empirical work does tend to produce numbers to report, so the parent habit is entangled with real quality and must appear in the undiscounted band too.
member_names: Density of specific numeric results reported
Density of specific quantified result figures

selected.name: Trend-Aligned Vocabulary
selected.instruction: How much does the abstract use recognizable fashionable terminology associated with currently prominent machine-learning themes? Score only the presence of trend vocabulary, not whether the topic is important or good.
selected.rationale: Submission timing can influence which topical labels and framing terms appear, without affecting research quality. Examples include robustness language in R04, world-model language in R24, and spectral-augmentation language in R52.

selected.name: Superlative Claim Rhetoric
selected.instruction: How much does the abstract use superlatives, priority claims, novelty claims, or emphatic comparative language such as first, novel, superior, remarkable, or state of the art? Score only rhetorical frequency, not truth or quality.
selected.rationale: Promotional claim density can influence reader salience without demonstrating research quality. It appears repeatedly in R10, R24, R42, and R60.

selected.name: Sheer expository volume of the abstract body
selected.instruction: Read only the abstract text and rate 0-10 how much total expository volume is present. Anchors: 0 = title only, or a single sentence of body text; 3 = roughly two to four sentences; 6 = one standard paragraph of about eight to twelve sentences; 10 = a long multi-part abstract of fifteen or more sentences covering several elaborated sub-topics. Count sentences, clauses, enumerated sub-points and number of distinct sub-topics touched. You are measuring QUANTITY OF TEXT ONLY. Do not judge whether the length is appropriate, whether the writing is clear or informative, or whether a short abstract is terse-and-confident versus thin. Longer is not better and shorter is not better; report extent only.
selected.rationale: Any scorecard built from a bank of explicit criteria can only fire on criteria whose evidence is literally written down, so raw token supply mechanically caps the achievable card score while a dense reader is free to price a terse text on its content. The slice shows exactly this asymmetry at both extremes: R06 has no abstract body at all (title only) and sits at card_pct=0.192 against dense_pct=0.521, and R24 is two sentences long with card_pct=0.321 against dense_pct=0.996 - the single largest disagreement in the slice. R27, R34 and R59 are likewise short and land card-low relative to dense. In the opposite direction the longest, most enumerative texts R14 (card 0.923) and R21 (card 0.974) sit far above their dense ranks. Word supply is a writing habit, not research quality.
member_names: Sheer expository volume of the abstract body

selected.name: Extent of adversarial/security-threat subject framing
selected.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how much the abstract centers on adversarial/security-threat framing -- attacks, adversarial examples, backdoors, poisoning, defenses, robustness certificates against a malicious actor. Score 0 if the topic has nothing to do with adversarial/security framing, and 10 if the entire abstract is organized around an attack-or-defense narrative. Do NOT judge whether this is an important or trendy topic to work on -- score only how much of the text is organized around this specific subject-matter framing.
selected.rationale: Seven of the dense_high_card_low rows in this slice are built around explicit attack/defense framing: R01 ('adversarial distortions', 'adversarial accuracy'), R26 ('Stochastic Activation Pruning for Robust Adversarial Defense'), R31 ('WaNet - Imperceptible Warping-based Backdoor Attack'), plus R12, R34, R44, and R53 -- none of this reflects the actual technical quality of the contribution, just a shared subject-matter cluster the dense model happens to rank high and the scorecard does not.

selected.name: Explicit first-to-achieve priority claims
selected.instruction: Read the abstract text only. Rate 0-10 how strongly the text makes an explicit claim to being first, novel-in-priority, or unprecedented (e.g., 'we are the first to...', 'for the first time', 'to the best of our knowledge, ... is the first'). Score 0 if no such priority claim appears, and 10 if the text makes an emphatic, explicit priority claim. Do NOT judge whether the priority claim is actually true or historically accurate -- score only whether this rhetorical claim is textually present.
selected.rationale: R01 states it can 'determine for the first time the exact adversarial accuracy of an MNIST classifier' (dense_pct=.987, card_pct=.444) and R54 states 'To the best of our knowledge, our approach is the first to achieve optimal deployment complexity and optimal d dependence ... at the same time' (dense_pct=.278, card_pct=.004, the lowest card_pct in the entire slice) -- both dense_high_card_low, suggesting explicit priority-claim rhetoric tracks the dense model's preference independent of whether the priority claim is itself substantiated.

selected.name: Publication-Polish Fluency
selected.instruction: How much does the abstract exhibit highly polished grammar, smooth transitions, standardized abstract structure, and publication-template fluency? Score only surface editing quality, not research quality.
selected.rationale: Professional editing can improve perceived clarity without changing the underlying research. Strongly conventional, polished presentation is visible in R24, R29, R40, and R42.

selected.name: Canonical Ecosystem Naming
selected.instruction: How much does the abstract name canonical datasets, benchmarks, architectures, standard methods, or well-known prior authors? Score only visible ecosystem references, not the importance of the work.
selected.rationale: Network access and institutional resources can shape familiarity with recognizable benchmarks and communities, while also plausibly supporting genuine quality. Examples include R02, R15, R37, and R57.
